title: Non-blocking kernel probe with timebox, telemetry, and graceful rollback
creator: Priya Nair
description:
Background: Our current synchronous kernel probing (probe native CUTLASS/Triton variants at startup) blocks runtime initialization and contributes to high cold-start latency and occasional unrecoverable failures on heterogenous fleets. Several incidents in Q1 showed probe hang/retry behavior on older driver combinations and experimental kernel builds. The long-term plan is to move to a staged kernel manifest + lazy loader, but that work is a multi-cycle refactor.

Goal: Implement a pragmatic, low-risk non-blocking probe that: (1) removes kernel probe from the critical path of runtime startup, (2) timeboxes probe attempts so a single flakey probe cannot stall the process, (3) surfaces rich telemetry to identify hosts with unstable kernel stacks, and (4) provides a clear graceful-rollback and fallback policy when a required kernel variant is unavailable. This ticket implements the non-blocking probe harness and rollout plan.

Proposed design:
- Move probe logic to a dedicated background worker thread pool initialized after minimal runtime is up. The worker will attempt to load requested kernel bundles but will not prevent serving on conservative execution paths.
- Timebox per-probe attempt to 350ms default; after N attempts (configurable, default 2) mark variant "probe-timed-out" for this host and fall back to the compatibility path (eg. scalar fallback or quantized generic kernels).
- Add a host-local probe cache with TTL (24h default) to avoid repeated probing storms during autoscaling events.
- Emit structured telemetry for each probe attempt: kernel_variant, elapsed_ms, outcome {success|timeout|link_error|symbol_conflict}, driver_version, os_release, host_id, probe_attempt_id. Ship to datadog as gauge+histogram + logs to S3 for forensic analysis.
- Expose a new runtime flag --probe-mode={blocking,nonblocking} for internal canary. Default for canary hosts: nonblocking.
- Integrate an automated remediation playbook: if a host reports >10% probe-timeout rate for the same variant in 6 hours, add host to quarantine pool and route new requests to alternate capacity.

Acceptance criteria:
- Runtime no longer stays blocked for >500ms waiting on kernel probe during initial warm start on canary hosts.
- Probe telemetry emitted for 100% of probe attempts (validated by test harness).
- Canary rollout to 5% of dedicated fleet without increase in P95 latency or error rate (SLOs hold).
- Automated quarantine triggers in test harness and a documented rollback procedure.

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for probe timeboxing and cache behaviour.
- Integration harness that injects simulated link errors and artificial long loads to validate fallback logic. Harness repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/gpu-probe-harness (WIP).
- Canary in staging with synthetic traffic and per-host telemetry dashboards: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/gpu-probe/new-probe-dashboard
- Preflight job in CI: run lightweight probe simulation on per-commit container with mocked LD_PRELOAD failures.

Rollout plan:
1) Merge feature behind runtime flag and default nonblocking only on internal canary cluster.
2) Monitor probe-timeout rates, cold-start p95, and error spike for 48h.
3) Expand to 5% of Dedicated capacity for 72h.
4) If stable, promote to 25% and run long-running workloads (24h).
5) Full fleet only after cross-team signoff.

Rollback: revert flag or set --probe-mode=blocking on affected fleet; quarantine policy will automatically redirect traffic away from hosts flagged by telemetry.

Risks & trade-offs:
- Non-blocking probe can hide an underlying incompatibility until a request triggers a slow fallback path. Mitigation: aggressive telemetry, synthetic health checks that exercise hot code paths.
- Timebox value requires tuning; too aggressive increases false negatives, too lenient keeps startup latency. We'll iterate using A/B telem.
